title: Inference versus training: completely different engineering problems
story:
The same weights are involved and almost nothing else is shared. Treating these as two modes of one activity is the source of a great many wrong expectations, so it is worth laying the differences out as differences in kind.

Training consumes a fixed dataset, so the work is known in advance. It can be scheduled, restarted, run overnight, and made to wait. Nobody is watching a particular step. The measure of success is a number going down, and the cost is dominated by arithmetic across an enormous number of examples, which makes the job a throughput problem: keep the hardware busy and finish sooner.

Inference receives requests as they arrive, so the work is unpredictable in both timing and size. Somebody is waiting for each one. The measure of success is a response that arrives soon enough and is good enough, and nothing about a previous request helps the next. That makes it a latency-under-uncertainty problem, and those are not the same discipline.

The memory picture is where the difference is most concrete, and it explains the thing people find surprising. Training must retain the intermediate values from the forward pass so the backward pass can consume them, which means memory scales with the depth of the network and the size of the batch. It also holds the gradients and whatever state the update rule keeps. Inference needs none of that: values can be discarded as soon as they have been used. So a model that cannot be trained on a machine may run on it comfortably, and the gap is not marginal — the training requirement is a multiple of the inference one.

Failure means different things too, which changes how each is engineered. A training run that dies can be resumed from a checkpoint and the only loss is time. A request that fails has failed for a person, and there is no checkpoint. So inference needs the whole apparatus of serving — timeouts, retries that do not duplicate effects, admission control, graceful refusal — and training needs almost none of it, while training needs reproducibility and checkpointing that inference has no use for.

The scaling axes are different in a way worth stating explicitly. Training scales by making one job bigger: more hardware working on the same problem, coordinating. Inference scales by running more copies of the same small job independently, which is easy, until the thing that binds is memory per copy rather than arithmetic — at which point the limit is how many concurrent requests fit, not how fast the hardware computes.

Which gives the asymmetry that explains most deployment surprises. Training cost is large, known in advance, and paid once. Inference cost is smaller per unit and paid on every request forever, so it scales with success. A model that is expensive to train and cheap to run and a model that is cheap to train and expensive to run are different products with different economics, and the second one gets more expensive precisely when it is going well.

The exception worth knowing, since the separation is otherwise clean: fine-tuning is training, with all of training's memory profile and none of its tolerance for taking a week. And anything that updates a model from live traffic collapses the distinction deliberately, which means it inherits both sets of problems rather than splitting the difference.

problem.name: Two different jobs
problem.shape: A model must both be produced and be used, and the two activities are being planned as one.
tell: hardware was sized for one of the two and is being used for the other
a model that trains fine is too slow to serve, or vice versa

problem.move: Plan them separately. Training is throughput on known work that can wait; inference is latency on unpredictable work that cannot. Size memory from the training requirement and concurrency from the inference one, and treat inference cost as growing with success rather than fixed.
problem.invariant: Training retains the forward pass's intermediate values for the backward pass, so its memory scales with depth and batch size; inference discards them immediately. The training requirement is a multiple of the inference one.
problem.breaks: The separation is clean until something crosses it. Fine-tuning has training's memory profile and none of its tolerance for taking a week, and anything updating a model from live traffic collapses the distinction deliberately — inheriting both sets of problems rather than splitting the difference.

cost.time: two sets of infrastructure concerns, with little reuse between them
cost.space: training hardware sized for retained intermediates, serving capacity sized for concurrent resident requests
cost.beats: sizing everything for training, which is safe and wastes serving capacity on memory nothing needs, and sizing everything for inference, which is cheap and cannot train the model at all

problem.practice: Take a model you can run locally and find its memory use while serving, then estimate what training it would require by accounting for retained intermediates, gradients and update state. The ratio is why the two jobs get different hardware.

beats.broke: Training and serving were planned as two modes of one activity, so hardware, failure handling and cost models sized for one were applied to the other.
beats.fix: Treat them as different disciplines: throughput on known work that can wait, versus latency on unpredictable work that cannot — and size memory from training, concurrency from serving.
beats.cost: Two sets of infrastructure concerns with little reuse, and the separation breaks wherever something crosses it, as fine-tuning and live updating both do.

interview.q: Why can a model that will not train on a machine often run on it comfortably?
interview.trap: Attributing it to arithmetic throughput. The binding difference is memory: training retains the forward pass's intermediates because the backward pass consumes them, and inference discards them immediately.
interview.answer:
Because training retains data that inference discards, and the difference is a multiple rather than a margin.

Training must keep the intermediate values from the forward pass, since the backward pass consumes them to compute gradients — so memory scales with the network's depth and the batch size, plus the gradients themselves and whatever state the update rule maintains. Inference needs none of it: a value is discarded the moment it has been used, because nothing will come back for it.

That memory gap is the most visible of several differences in kind. The work has a different shape: training consumes a fixed dataset, so the work is known in advance and can be scheduled, restarted and made to wait, with nobody watching a particular step — a throughput problem. Inference takes requests as they arrive, unpredictable in timing and size, with somebody waiting and nothing about a previous request helping the next — a latency-under-uncertainty problem.

Failure differs too: a training run that dies resumes from a checkpoint and loses only time, while a failed request has failed for a person and there is no checkpoint. So serving needs timeouts, non-duplicating retries, admission control and graceful refusal, and training needs reproducibility and checkpointing that serving has no use for.

The scaling axes differ: training makes one job bigger with hardware coordinating on the same problem, while inference runs more copies independently — easy until the binding constraint is memory per copy rather than arithmetic, at which point the limit is how many concurrent requests fit.

And the asymmetry that explains most deployment surprises: training cost is large, known in advance and paid once, while inference cost is smaller per unit and paid on every request forever, so it scales with success — which means it gets more expensive precisely when things are going well.

The exception is fine-tuning, which is training with training's memory profile and none of its tolerance for taking a week; and anything updating a model from live traffic collapses the distinction and inherits both sets of problems.
